q: The maximum consumption of a material is 560 units per week, the normal consumption is 360 units per week and the maximum lead time is 4 weeks. The safety stock, computed as (Maximum consumption - Normal consumption) x Maximum lead time, is:
e: Safety stock covers consumption above normal during the maximum lead time: (560 - 360) x 4 = 200 x 4 = 800 units.

q: The annual consumption of a material is 16,200 units. The cost of placing an order is Rs 100 and the carrying cost is Rs 4 per unit per year. Using EOQ = sqrt(2AO/C), the Economic Order Quantity is:
e: EOQ balances ordering cost against carrying cost: sqrt(2 x 16,200 x 100 / 4) = sqrt(8,10,000) = 900 units.

q: In inventory control, under SDE analysis, stores items are classified as Scarce, Difficult and Easy on the basis of:

options.B: Their criticality for production or services
options.C: The speed of their movement from the stores
options.D: Their availability and the ease or difficulty of procuring them — scarce items being hard to obtain, often imported or in short supply

e: SDE analysis classifies items by availability: Scarce items are hard to obtain (often imported or in short supply), Difficult items are not readily available, and Easy items are freely available.

q: The annual credit sales of an enterprise are Rs 18,00,000 and its average debtors are Rs 1,80,000. Taking a year of 360 days, the average collection period is:
e: Average collection period = Average debtors / Credit sales x 360 = 1,80,000 / 18,00,000 x 360 = 36 days.

q: Annual credit purchases of an enterprise are Rs 16,50,000 and its average creditors are Rs 3,30,000. The creditors turnover ratio is:
e: Creditors turnover = Credit purchases / Average creditors = 16,50,000 / 3,30,000 = 5 times, showing how often creditors are paid off in the year.

q: A supplier offers credit terms of 2/20, net 60. The approximate annual cost of not taking the cash discount (on a 360-day year basis) is:
e: Cost of forgoing the discount = 2/98 x 360 / (60 - 20) = 2.04% x 9 = 18.4% per annum approximately.

q: The credit terms '5/10, net 60' offered by a supplier mean that:

options.A: Interest at 5% is charged if payment is made after 10 days
options.B: The buyer must pay 5% of the invoice value within 10 days and the balance within 60 days
options.C: A discount of 60% is allowed if payment is made within 5 days
options.D: A cash discount of 5% is allowed if payment is made within 10 days; otherwise the full invoice amount is payable within 60 days

e: In '5/10, net 60', the first figure is the cash discount rate, the second the discount period, and 'net 60' the full credit period: 5% off if paid within 10 days, else the full amount within 60 days.

q: 'Discounting of bills', as a means of financing receivables, means:

options.A: Getting the firm's bills of exchange discounted with a bank before maturity — the bank credits the firm with the face value less discount for the unexpired period, so that the firm receives funds immediately instead of waiting for the due date
options.B: Allowing customers a cash discount for early payment
options.C: Writing off bills which have become irrecoverable
options.D: Selling the receivables outright to a factor, who assumes the risk of bad debts

e: In discounting, the bank pays the firm the face value of its bills less discount for the unexpired period, so the firm gets funds at once instead of waiting till maturity.

q: Under the Baumol model of cash management, an enterprise's annual cash requirement is Rs 49,00,000, the cost of converting marketable securities into cash is Rs 40 per transaction and the opportunity interest rate is 8% per annum. The optimum cash balance, sqrt(2AT/i), is:
e: Baumol optimum cash balance = sqrt(2AT/i) = sqrt(2 x 49,00,000 x 40 / 0.08) = sqrt(4,90,00,00,000) = Rs 70,000.

q: Under the Miller-Orr model of cash management, an enterprise fixes a lower control limit of Rs 40,000 and a spread of Rs 1,20,000 between the control limits. The return point (target cash balance) is:
e: Under Miller-Orr, the return point lies one-third of the spread above the lower limit: 40,000 + 1,20,000 / 3 = 40,000 + 40,000 = Rs 80,000.

q: In cash management, the expression 'playing the float' refers to:

options.A: Investing the surplus cash of the firm in marketable securities
options.B: Maintaining a minimum cash balance with the bank at all times
options.C: Preparing the cash budget on the basis of estimated floats
options.D: The practice of issuing cheques in excess of the balance actually available, relying on the time taken in clearing them and on deposits yet to be cleared — a risky practice which may amount to cheque kiting

e: 'Float' is the gap between the bank balance and the book balance caused by cheques issued but not yet presented and deposits not yet cleared; playing the float means issuing cheques against uncleared funds, a risky practice akin to cheque kiting.

q: While selecting marketable securities for parking temporary surplus cash, the consideration which should rank first is:

options.A: Safety of the principal and ready marketability (liquidity), even if the yield is comparatively low
options.B: The highest possible rate of return, whatever the risk involved
options.D: Exemption of the income from income tax

e: Surplus cash is parked only temporarily, so safety of principal and ready marketability come first; yield is secondary because the funds may be needed at short notice.

q: A division earns a profit of Rs 12,35,000 on capital employed of Rs 65,00,000. The Return on Investment of the division is:
e: ROI = Profit / Capital employed x 100 = 12,35,000 / 65,00,000 x 100 = 19%.

q: A division earns a profit of Rs 17,00,000 on capital employed of Rs 1,10,00,000. The cost of capital is 12%. The Residual Income of the division is:
e: Residual Income = Profit - Cost of capital x Capital employed = 17,00,000 - 12% of 1,10,00,000 = 17,00,000 - 13,20,000 = Rs 3,80,000.

q: The Net Operating Profit After Tax (NOPAT) of a division is Rs 21,00,000, its capital employed is Rs 1,50,00,000 and the cost of capital is 11%. Its Economic Value Added (EVA) is:
Economic Value Added (EVA) differs from the traditional Residual Income measure mainly in that EVA:

options.A: Is computed on the net operating profit after tax, uses the weighted average cost of capital for the capital charge, and is generally arrived at after making a number of adjustments to the reported accounting profit and capital
options.B: Ignores the cost of capital altogether
options.C: Is expressed always as a percentage and never as an absolute amount
options.D: Can be computed only by companies listed on a stock exchange

e: EVA refines residual income: it starts from net operating profit after tax, charges capital at the weighted average cost of capital, and adjusts reported profit and capital (e.g. for R and D, provisions) to approximate economic profit.

q: The Market Value Added (MVA) of an enterprise is conceptually equal to:

options.A: The economic value added generated by it in the current year alone
options.B: The present value of all the Economic Value Added (EVA) expected to be generated by the enterprise in the future
options.C: The book value of its net assets
options.D: The excess of its market capitalisation over its paid-up share capital alone

e: MVA is the market's cumulative assessment of value created; conceptually it equals the discounted value of all EVA the enterprise is expected to earn in future years.

q: In transfer pricing, the 'arm's length price' is:

options.A: The price fixed by the head office for all inter-divisional transfers
options.B: The cost of production plus a fixed percentage of profit
options.C: The price which would be charged for the same or a similar product in a transaction between independent, unrelated parties dealing with each other freely
options.D: The average of the market price and the cost of production

e: An arm's length price is the price that independent, unrelated parties would agree for the same or a similar product in the open market, free from the influence of their relationship.

q: The expected market price of a product is Rs 900 per unit and the firm desires a profit of 20% on cost. The target cost of the product is:
e: Target cost = Expected price / (1 + Profit on cost) = 900 / 1.20 = Rs 750; the production cost must be engineered down to this allowable level.

q: The actual cost of a product in the previous period was Rs 1,200 per unit. Under kaizen costing, a cost-reduction target of 4% is set for the current period. The kaizen target cost for the current period is:
e: Kaizen costing pursues continuous small reductions from the existing cost base: 1,200 - 4% of 1,200 = 1,200 - 48 = Rs 1,152.

q: The costing technique known in Japan as 'genka kikaku', under which the allowable cost of a new product is derived from the price the market will bear and the profit required, is:
e: Genka kikaku is the Japanese name for target costing, where the allowable cost of a new product is derived at the design stage from the market price minus the required profit.

q: In value engineering, the 'worth' of a function is understood to be:

options.A: The price at which the product can be sold in the market
options.B: The actual cost presently incurred in performing the function
options.C: The lowest cost at which the function can reliably be performed by any known means — a comparison of the present cost with the worth reveals the scope for cost reduction
options.D: The total life-cycle cost of the product

e: Worth is the lowest cost at which a function can be reliably performed by any known means; comparing present cost with worth shows the value gap that value engineering seeks to close.

q: 'Backflush costing', used in just-in-time production environments, is a system under which:

options.A: Costs are accumulated separately for every job order as production proceeds
options.B: All material issues are recorded in detail at the point of issue to production
options.C: A buffer stock of work-in-progress is deliberately maintained at every stage
options.D: Product costs are applied (flushed back) only when production is completed, or the goods are sold, using predetermined rates, so that detailed tracking of costs through work-in-progress is dispensed with

e: Backflush costing delays cost recording until output is completed or sold, then flushes costs back using predetermined rates, avoiding detailed tracking through work-in-progress in a JIT setting.

q: 'Benchmarking', as a technique of performance improvement, means:

options.A: Comparing the products, processes and performance measures of the organisation with those of the best-performing (best-in-class) organisations, in order to identify the gaps and adopt the best practices
options.B: Fixing the standard cost of a product for the coming year
options.C: Marking the benches in the factory for quality inspection
options.D: Comparing the actual results of the year with the budget of the same year

e: Benchmarking compares products, processes and performance measures with best-in-class organisations to identify performance gaps and adopt the best practices that close them.

q: An 'operational audit' is concerned with:

options.A: The audit of the financial statements by the statutory auditor
options.B: A systematic review of the operations and processes of an organisation, or a part of it, to appraise their efficiency, economy and effectiveness with a view to improving performance
options.C: The audit of the personal accounts of the officers of the organisation
options.D: The verification of the physical existence of the fixed assets

e: Operational audit appraises the efficiency, economy and effectiveness of operations and processes (the three Es), going beyond financial verification to suggest performance improvement.

q: The sales of a factory for a period are Rs 12,00,000 and the totally variable costs (direct materials) are Rs 5,40,000. All other factory costs are treated as operating expenses. The throughput for the period is:
e: Under throughput accounting, only totally variable costs (here direct materials) are deducted from sales: 12,00,000 - 5,40,000 = Rs 6,60,000; all other factory costs are operating expenses of the period.

q: In the Theory of Constraints, after the system's constraint has been identified, the second of the five focusing steps requires management to:

options.A: Exploit the constraint — to get the maximum possible output from the constraint resource, ensuring that it is never kept idle and is not wasted on work which does not generate throughput
options.B: Immediately purchase additional capacity for the constraint resource
options.C: Subordinate the sales programme of the enterprise to its production programme
options.D: Search for the next constraint in the system

e: The second focusing step is to exploit the constraint: squeeze maximum throughput from the bottleneck, never let it stand idle or waste its time on non-throughput work, before spending on extra capacity.

q: In the 'drum-buffer-rope' system of production scheduling based on the Theory of Constraints:

options.A: The 'drum' is the storekeeper who releases materials to the shops
options.B: The 'rope' is the physical conveyor linking all the work stations
options.C: The 'buffer' is the finished-goods godown of the factory
options.D: The 'drum' is the pace set by the bottleneck (constraint) resource, which determines the rate at which the whole system works; the 'buffer' protects the constraint from starvation, and the 'rope' ties the release of materials to the pace of the constraint

e: In drum-buffer-rope, the constraint sets the drumbeat (pace) for the whole plant, a time buffer of work protects it from starvation, and the rope links material release to its pace.

q: An asset was purchased for Rs 1,50,000 when the general price index stood at 90. At the balance sheet date the index stands at 150. Under the Current Purchasing Power (CPP) method, the restated value of the asset is:
e: Under CPP, non-monetary items are restated by the index change: 1,50,000 x 150 / 90 = Rs 2,50,000.

q: In Current Cost Accounting (CCA), the 'depreciation adjustment' represents:

options.A: The depreciation charged on assets which have been revalued upward for the first time
options.B: The difference between the historical cost of the assets and their written-down value
options.C: The excess of the depreciation required on the current replacement cost (value to the business) of the fixed assets over the depreciation charged on their historical cost, representing the additional amount needed to maintain the operating capability of the enterprise
options.D: The amount of depreciation disallowed under the Income-tax Act

e: Under CCA, depreciation based on current replacement cost exceeds historical-cost depreciation; the difference is the depreciation adjustment, the extra charge needed to maintain the firm's operating capability.

q: Under XYZ analysis for selective control of inventory, stores items are classified into X, Y and Z categories primarily on the basis of:

options.A: The value of the inventory (stock) held of the items
options.B: The annual consumption value of the items
options.C: The criticality of the items for production
options.D: The rate of consumption of the items

e: XYZ analysis classifies items by the value of stock held: X items tie up the highest inventory value, Z the lowest, guiding the strictness of stock control.

q: Under SDE analysis for selective control of inventory, stores items are classified as Scarce, Difficult and Easy primarily on the basis of:

options.A: The ease or difficulty of procuring (availability of) the items

e: SDE analysis groups items as Scarce, Difficult or Easy according to how easily they can be procured, so that scarce items get special procurement attention.

q: The maximum consumption of a material is 320 units per week and the maximum delivery (lead) period is 6 weeks. The re-order level of the material is:
e: Re-order level = Maximum consumption x Maximum lead time = 320 x 6 = 1,920 units, the level at which a fresh order must be placed.

q: The re-order level of a material is 2,900 units and the re-order quantity is 1,600 units. The minimum consumption is 150 units per week and the minimum delivery period is 4 weeks. The maximum stock level of the material is:
e: Maximum stock level = Re-order level + Re-order quantity - (Minimum consumption x Minimum lead time) = 2,900 + 1,600 - (150 x 4) = 4,500 - 600 = 3,900 units.

q: The re-order level of a material is 5,200 units. The normal consumption is 350 units per week and the normal delivery period is 6 weeks. The minimum stock level of the material is:
e: Minimum stock level = Re-order level - (Normal consumption x Normal lead time) = 5,200 - (350 x 6) = 5,200 - 2,100 = 3,100 units.

q: The annual consumption of a material is 4,050 units. The cost of placing an order is Rs 100 and the carrying cost is Rs 4 per unit per year. Using EOQ = sqrt(2AO/C), the Economic Order Quantity is:
e: EOQ = sqrt(2 x 4,050 x 100 / 4) = sqrt(2,02,500) = 450 units, where total ordering cost equals total carrying cost.

q: Under the replacement price method of pricing material issues, stores are issued to production at:

options.A: The price at which the material was originally purchased
options.B: The average price of all the lots held in stock
options.C: A predetermined standard price fixed for the period
options.D: The current market (replacement) price prevailing on the date of issue

e: Under the replacement price method, each issue is priced at the market price prevailing on the date of issue, so production is charged with the current cost of replacing the material.

q: 'Spoilage' in production refers to units which:

options.A: Do not conform to the prescribed standards but can be rectified and made good at some extra cost
options.B: Are damaged while lying in the stores, before being issued to production
options.C: Are produced in excess of the quantity ordered
options.D: Do not conform to the prescribed standards, cannot be rectified economically, and are disposed of at their scrap or disposal value

e: Defective units that can be rectified are rework; spoilage is output so defective it cannot be rectified economically and is disposed of only for its scrap value.

q: Royalty payable by a manufacturer on the basis of the number of units SOLD is treated in cost accounts as:

options.A: A direct expense forming part of prime cost
options.D: An item excluded from the cost accounts

e: Royalty based on units sold varies with sales, not production, so it is a selling and distribution overhead; royalty on units produced would be a direct expense.

q: Under Merrick's multiple piece-rate system, a worker whose efficiency is below 83% of the standard is paid at the ordinary piece rate, efficiency between 83% and 100% is paid at 110% of the ordinary rate, and efficiency above 100% is paid at 120% of the ordinary rate. The ordinary piece rate is Rs 4 per unit and the standard output is 100 units per day. A worker who produces 95 units in a day will earn:
e: Output 95 units is 95% efficiency, attracting 110% of the ordinary rate under Merrick's plan: 95 x Rs 4 x 1.10 = Rs 418.

q: Under the Bedaux plan, a worker is paid time wages for the time taken plus a premium equal to 75% of the wages of the time saved, time being measured in B-units (points). The standard time allowed for a job is 480 B-units (8 hours) and a worker completes it in 6 hours. The wage rate is Rs 60 per hour. His total earnings are:
e: Time taken 6 hours earns 6 x 60 = Rs 360; time saved is 120 B-units = 2 hours, premium 75% x 2 x 60 = Rs 90; total = Rs 450.

q: A worker is paid a piece rate of Rs 12 per unit, subject to a guaranteed minimum wage of Rs 2,500 per week. If he produces 180 units in a week, his total earnings for the week are:
e: Piece earnings = 180 x Rs 12 = Rs 2,160, which is below the guaranteed minimum of Rs 2,500, so the worker is paid Rs 2,500 for the week.

q: Overtime is worked in a factory to make up for the production lost on account of a fire in the plant. In cost accounts, the overtime premium paid for such work is:

options.A: Charged to the jobs completed during the overtime hours
options.B: Treated as a general factory overhead
options.C: Treated as an abnormal loss and transferred to the Costing Profit and Loss Account
options.D: Added to the cost of the assets damaged by the fire

e: Overtime premium arising from an abnormal cause like fire is not a normal production cost; it is treated as abnormal loss and transferred to the Costing Profit and Loss Account.

q: Which of the following is a NON-financial incentive for workers?

options.D: Recognition of good work and opportunities for promotion

e: Bonus, profit-sharing and dearness allowance are all monetary; recognition of good work and promotion opportunities are non-financial incentives that satisfy esteem and growth needs.

q: The production-unit (output) method of absorbing factory overheads is most suitable where:

options.B: A large number of dissimilar jobs are executed
options.C: Labour is the dominant factor of production
options.D: Only a single product, or substantially uniform units, are produced

e: The production-unit method (overhead rate per unit) works only when output consists of a single product or substantially uniform units, so each unit can fairly bear the same overhead.

q: Under the normal capacity concept (Ind AS 2), where the actual production in a period is abnormally LOW, the fixed production overheads are allocated to the cost of production:

options.A: On the basis of normal capacity, and the unallocated fixed overheads are recognised as an expense of the period
options.B: By increasing the overhead rate per unit so that all the fixed overheads are absorbed
options.C: By carrying forward the unabsorbed overheads to the next period
options.D: By adding them to the value of the closing stock

e: Under Ind AS 2, fixed production overheads are allocated on normal capacity; when actual output is abnormally low, the unallocated overhead is expensed in the period rather than loaded into stock.

q: An all-inclusive (comprehensive) machine hour rate, as distinguished from the ordinary machine hour rate, additionally includes:

options.B: The rent of the factory building
options.C: The cost of power consumed by the machine
options.D: The wages of the machine operator

e: The ordinary machine hour rate covers machine costs including the operator only if separately added; the all-inclusive (comprehensive) rate additionally includes the machine operator's wages.

q: A machine is used for 2,400 hours in a year. Its standing charges for the year are Rs 45,000 and its running charges are Rs 75,000. The machine hour rate is:
e: Machine hour rate = (Standing charges + Running charges) / Machine hours = (45,000 + 75,000) / 2,400 = 1,20,000 / 2,400 = Rs 50 per hour.

q: Fixed production overheads of a factory are Rs 96,000 and production during the period is 12,000 units. The opening stock of finished goods is 1,500 units and the closing stock is 2,500 units. Compared with marginal costing, the profit under absorption costing for the period will be:

options.D: The same as under marginal costing

e: Fixed overhead rate = 96,000 / 12,000 = Rs 8 per unit. Stock rises by 2,500 - 1,500 = 1,000 units, so absorption costing defers 1,000 x 8 = Rs 8,000 more fixed cost in stock, making its profit higher by Rs 8,000.

q: A recognised criticism of absorption costing is that, under it, the profit of a period can be increased merely by:

options.A: Increasing the selling price of the product
options.B: Reducing the variable cost per unit
options.C: Increasing production and building up stocks, even without any increase in sales
options.D: Reducing the fixed overheads of the period

e: Under absorption costing, fixed overheads are carried into closing stock, so producing more than is sold defers fixed costs and inflates the period's profit without any increase in sales.

q: A product sells for Rs 85 per unit and its variable cost is Rs 51 per unit. Fixed costs are Rs 2,38,000. The break-even point in units is:
e: BEP in units = Fixed costs / Contribution per unit = 2,38,000 / (85 - 51) = 2,38,000 / 34 = 7,000 units.

q: The P/V ratio of a firm is 32% and its fixed costs are Rs 2,40,000. Its break-even sales are:
e: BEP sales = Fixed costs / P/V ratio = 2,40,000 / 32% = Rs 7,50,000.

q: A product sells for Rs 160 per unit with a variable cost of Rs 112 per unit. Fixed costs are Rs 2,88,000. The number of units to be sold to earn a target profit of Rs 96,000 is:
e: Units for target profit = (Fixed costs + Target profit) / Contribution per unit = (2,88,000 + 96,000) / (160 - 112) = 3,84,000 / 48 = 8,000 units.

q: A firm sells two products: P with sales of Rs 5,00,000 and a P/V ratio of 30%, and Q with sales of Rs 3,00,000 and a P/V ratio of 50%. Total fixed costs are Rs 2,40,000. The overall break-even sales of the firm are:
The fixed costs of a firm are Rs 3,00,000, which include depreciation of Rs 60,000. The P/V ratio is 30%. The cash break-even sales of the firm are:
e: Cash fixed costs exclude depreciation: 3,00,000 - 60,000 = 2,40,000. Cash BEP sales = 2,40,000 / 30% = Rs 8,00,000, the sales needed to cover cash costs only.

q: Labour hours are the limiting factor in a factory. Product A gives a contribution of Rs 88 per unit and requires 4 labour hours per unit; Product B gives a contribution of Rs 99 per unit and requires 6 labour hours per unit. To maximise profit, production priority should be given to:

options.A: Product A, because its contribution per labour hour (Rs 22) is higher
options.B: Product B, because its contribution per unit (Rs 99) is higher
options.C: Product B, because its contribution per labour hour is higher
options.D: Both products equally, as their total contribution is the same

e: With labour hours limiting, rank by contribution per labour hour: A gives 88 / 4 = Rs 22 per hour against B's 99 / 6 = Rs 16.50, so A gets priority despite its lower contribution per unit.

q: A factory has 24,000 machine hours available. Product A, which ranks first on the basis of contribution per machine hour, requires 8 machine hours per unit and its maximum demand is 2,200 units. Product B requires 8 machine hours per unit. After meeting the full demand for A, the number of units of B that can be produced is:
e: A uses 2,200 x 8 = 17,600 of the 24,000 hours, leaving 6,400 hours; B needs 8 hours per unit, so B output = 6,400 / 8 = 800 units.

q: The total fixed costs of a plant are Rs 4,80,000 per year, of which Rs 1,90,000 would continue to be incurred even during a shutdown. Shutdown (discontinuance) costs of Rs 30,000 would also be incurred if the plant is closed. The contribution is Rs 32 per unit. The shutdown point of the plant is:
e: Shutdown point = (Avoidable fixed costs + Shutdown costs) / Contribution per unit = [(4,80,000 - 1,90,000) + 30,000] / 32 = 3,20,000 / 32 = 10,000 units; below this output, shutting down loses less.

q: A joint product can be sold at the split-off point for Rs 72 per unit. It can alternatively be processed further at an additional cost of Rs 25 per unit and then sold for Rs 104 per unit. The correct decision is to:

options.A: Sell at the split-off point, as the further processing cost is high in relation to the split-off price
options.B: Process further, as the incremental revenue of Rs 32 per unit exceeds the further processing cost of Rs 25 per unit
options.C: Sell at the split-off point, because the joint cost is a sunk cost
options.D: Process further only if the whole of the joint cost is recovered

e: Joint cost at split-off is sunk. Incremental revenue from further processing = 104 - 72 = Rs 32 per unit, exceeding the Rs 25 further processing cost, so processing further adds Rs 7 per unit.

q: In a process, 6,000 units are introduced at a total cost of Rs 1,41,000. Normal loss is 10% of the input and the scrap realises Rs 10 per unit. The cost per unit of good output is:
In a process, 7,500 units are introduced and the normal loss is 8% of the input. The actual output obtained is 6,750 units. The abnormal loss is:
e: Expected output = 7,500 - 8% of 7,500 = 7,500 - 600 = 6,900 units. Actual output 6,750 is less, so abnormal loss = 6,900 - 6,750 = 150 units.

q: In a process, 4,200 units were completed and transferred to the next process during a period. The closing work-in-progress is 900 units, which are 60% complete in respect of all cost elements, and there was no opening work-in-progress. The equivalent production for the period is:
e: Equivalent production = Completed units + (Closing WIP x Degree of completion) = 4,200 + 900 x 60% = 4,200 + 540 = 4,740 units.

q: A joint cost of Rs 3,60,000 is to be apportioned between joint products A and B on the basis of their net realisable values (final sales value less further processing costs). A can be sold for Rs 5,20,000 after further processing costing Rs 80,000; B can be sold for Rs 3,00,000 after further processing costing Rs 1,40,000. The share of joint cost borne by A is:
In process costing, where a by-product has some saleable value, the amount realised from its sale is generally:

options.A: Treated as a miscellaneous income of the business
options.B: Added to the sales value of the main product for the purpose of pricing
options.C: Credited to the process account, thereby reducing the cost of the main product
options.D: Credited to the Costing Profit and Loss Account as an abnormal gain

e: Sale proceeds of a by-product are credited to the process account, reducing the cost borne by the main product, since the by-product arises incidentally from the same process.

q: An 'ideal standard' in standard costing is a standard which:

options.A: Is based on the average performance of the past few years
options.B: Can be attained only under the most favourable conditions, with maximum efficiency and no avoidable loss or idle time
options.C: Is attainable under normal efficient working conditions
options.D: Is fixed once and is never revised thereafter

e: An ideal standard assumes perfect conditions - maximum efficiency, no avoidable loss or idle time - and is attainable only in the most favourable circumstances, unlike the expected standard based on normal efficient working.

q: The standard price of a material is Rs 36 per kg and the actual price paid is Rs 39 per kg. The actual quantity consumed is 1,250 kg. The material price variance is:
e: Material price variance = (Standard price - Actual price) x Actual quantity = (36 - 39) x 1,250 = Rs 3,750 (Adverse), since more than standard price was paid.

q: For the actual output, the standard quantity of material is 1,350 kg, but the actual quantity consumed is 1,500 kg. The standard price is Rs 18 per kg. The material usage variance is:
e: Material usage variance = (Standard quantity - Actual quantity) x Standard price = (1,350 - 1,500) x 18 = Rs 2,700 (Adverse), reflecting excess consumption of 150 kg.

q: The standard mix for a batch of 100 kg is: Material X — 50 kg at Rs 14 per kg and Material Y — 50 kg at Rs 22 per kg. The actual mix used for the same batch is X — 40 kg and Y — 60 kg. The material mix variance is:
e: Standard cost of standard mix = 50 x 14 + 50 x 22 = Rs 1,800; actual mix at standard prices = 40 x 14 + 60 x 22 = Rs 1,880. Mix variance = 1,800 - 1,880 = Rs 80 (Adverse).

q: A process has a standard yield of 160 kg of output from 200 kg of input, the input costing Rs 30 per kg. The actual output obtained from 200 kg of input is 150 kg. The material yield variance is:
e: Standard cost per kg of output = (200 x 30) / 160 = Rs 37.50. Yield shortfall = 160 - 150 = 10 kg, so yield variance = 10 x 37.50 = Rs 375 (Adverse).

q: The standard wage rate is Rs 38 per hour and the actual rate paid is Rs 35 per hour for 1,400 actual hours worked. The labour rate variance is:
e: Labour rate variance = (Standard rate - Actual rate) x Actual hours = (38 - 35) x 1,400 = Rs 4,200 (Favourable), as labour was paid less than the standard rate.

q: For the actual output, the standard labour time is 2,400 hours, but only 2,250 hours were actually taken. The standard wage rate is Rs 30 per hour. The labour efficiency variance is:
e: Labour efficiency variance = (Standard hours - Actual hours) x Standard rate = (2,400 - 2,250) x 30 = Rs 4,500 (Favourable), since the work took fewer hours than standard.

q: In a factory, 120 hours were lost as idle time. The standard wage rate is Rs 36 per hour. The idle time variance is:

options.D: Nil, as idle time is not recorded in standard costing

e: Idle time is paid but produces nothing, so idle time variance = Idle hours x Standard rate = 120 x 36 = Rs 4,320, always adverse.

q: The standard variable overhead rate is Rs 8 per hour. The standard time for the actual output is 750 hours, but 1,450 hours were actually worked. The variable overhead efficiency variance is:
e: Variable overhead efficiency variance = (Standard hours - Actual hours) x Standard rate = (750 - 1,450) x 8 = Rs 5,600 (Adverse), because 700 excess hours were worked.

q: The budgeted production of a factory is 40,000 units and the standard fixed overhead rate is Rs 5 per unit. Actual production is 36,000 units. The fixed overhead volume variance is:
e: Fixed overhead volume variance = (Budgeted output - Actual output) x Standard rate = (40,000 - 36,000) x 5 = Rs 20,000 (Adverse), fixed overheads being under-absorbed on lower output.

q: The budgeted sales of a product are 7,200 units and the actual sales are 6,600 units. The standard profit margin is Rs 21 per unit. The sales margin volume variance is:
e: Sales margin volume variance = (Budgeted sales - Actual sales) x Standard profit margin = (7,200 - 6,600) x 21 = Rs 12,600 (Adverse), as 600 fewer units were sold.

q: A project requires an initial outlay of Rs 4,50,000 and is expected to yield a net cash inflow of Rs 1,50,000 at the end of each of the next 5 years. The cumulative present value (annuity) factor for 5 years at 9% is 3.890. The Net Present Value of the project is:
e: NPV = 1,50,000 x 3.890 - 4,50,000 = 5,83,500 - 4,50,000 = Rs 1,33,500; the positive NPV means the project earns more than the 9% discount rate.

q: A project requires an initial outlay of Rs 6,50,000. Its net cash inflows are Rs 3,00,000 at the end of Year 1 (present value factor at 14% = 0.877), Rs 3,00,000 at the end of Year 2 (present value factor at 14% = 0.769) and Rs 2,50,000 at the end of Year 3 (present value factor at 14% = 0.675). The Net Present Value of the project is:
The present value of Rs 3,00,000 receivable at the end of 3 years, discounted at 8% (present value factor 0.794), is:
e: Present value = Amount x PV factor = 3,00,000 x 0.794 = Rs 2,38,200.

q: Rs 1,50,000 invested today at 8% per annum compound interest will grow in 3 years to (the compound value factor for 3 years at 8% is 1.260):
e: Compound value = Principal x Compound value factor = 1,50,000 x 1.260 = Rs 1,89,000.

q: A machine costing Rs 12,60,000 generates a net cash inflow of Rs 1,80,000 per year. Its payback period is:
e: Payback period = Initial cost / Annual cash inflow = 12,60,000 / 1,80,000 = 7 years, the time to recover the investment from inflows.

q: A project costing Rs 4,80,000 yields net cash inflows of Rs 1,20,000 in Year 1, Rs 1,80,000 in Year 2, Rs 1,20,000 in Year 3 and Rs 1,20,000 in Year 4. Its payback period is:
e: Cumulative inflows: Year 1 = 1,20,000, Year 2 = 3,00,000, Year 3 = 4,20,000. Balance 60,000 of the 4,80,000 outlay comes from Year 4 inflow of 1,20,000, taking half a year: payback = 3 years 6 months.

q: A project involves an initial outlay of Rs 6,40,000. The discounted (present) values of its cash inflows are Rs 1,60,000 at the end of each of Year 1, Year 2, Year 3 and Year 4. The discounted payback period of the project is:
e: Discounted inflows total 1,60,000 x 4 = Rs 6,40,000, exactly recovering the outlay only at the end of Year 4, so the discounted payback period is 4 years.

q: A project's Net Present Value is (+) Rs 9,000 at a discount rate of 13% and (-) Rs 6,000 at a discount rate of 17%. By interpolation, its internal rate of return is approximately:
The present value of the future cash inflows of a project is Rs 8,40,000 and its initial investment is Rs 8,00,000. The Profitability Index of the project is:
e: Profitability Index = PV of inflows / Initial investment = 8,40,000 / 8,00,000 = 1.05; above 1, so the project is acceptable.

q: An investment of Rs 20,00,000 is expected to yield an average annual profit after depreciation and tax of Rs 1,80,000. The Average Rate of Return on the initial investment is:
e: ARR on initial investment = Average annual profit / Initial investment x 100 = 1,80,000 / 20,00,000 x 100 = 9%.

q: An investment of Rs 16,00,000 has an expected salvage value of Rs 4,00,000 at the end of its life, so that the average investment over its life is Rs 10,00,000. If the average annual profit after depreciation and tax is Rs 1,60,000, the Average Rate of Return computed on the average investment is:
If the Net Present Value of a project, computed at the enterprise's cost of capital, is exactly zero, it means that:

options.A: The project will earn no profit at all during its life
options.B: The project should be rejected because it adds nothing to the enterprise
options.C: The internal rate of return of the project is zero
options.D: The internal rate of return of the project is equal to the cost of capital and its profitability index is exactly 1

e: NPV of zero means inflows discounted at the cost of capital exactly equal the outlay, so the project just earns the cost of capital: its IRR equals that rate and its profitability index is 1.

q: A company's capital structure consists of equity capital of Rs 10,00,000 (cost 14%), preference capital of Rs 5,00,000 (cost 10%) and debt of Rs 5,00,000 (after-tax cost 6%). Its weighted average cost of capital is:
A company's capital structure consists of debt of Rs 8,00,000 with an after-tax cost of 9% and equity of Rs 12,00,000 with a cost of 14%. Its weighted average cost of capital is:
A company issues 14% debentures at par. If the tax rate is 25%, the after-tax cost of debt is:
e: Interest is tax-deductible, so after-tax cost of debt = 14% x (1 - 0.25) = 10.5%.

q: A company issues 13% preference shares of face value Rs 100 each at Rs 104 per share. The cost of preference capital is:
e: Cost of preference capital = Dividend / Net proceeds = 13 / 104 = 12.5%, the dividend being fixed on face value while the firm receives Rs 104 per share.

q: A share is expected to pay a dividend of Rs 7 per share next year. Its market price is Rs 56 and dividends are expected to grow at a constant rate of 5% per year. Using the dividend growth model, the cost of equity is:
e: By the dividend growth model, cost of equity = D1 / P0 + g = 7 / 56 + 5% = 12.5% + 5% = 17.5%.

q: Using the Capital Asset Pricing Model, where the risk-free rate is 8%, the expected market return is 15% and the beta of the share is 1.4, the cost of equity is:
e: By CAPM, cost of equity = Rf + Beta x (Rm - Rf) = 8% + 1.4 x (15 - 8)% = 8% + 9.8% = 17.8%.

q: Under Walter's model of dividend policy, where the return on investment (r) earned by the firm is higher than its cost of capital (k), the dividend payout ratio which maximises the market price of the share is:

options.D: Any payout ratio, as the market price is unaffected by the payout

e: Under Walter's model, when the firm earns more on retained earnings (r) than shareholders require (k), retention creates value, so the price-maximising payout is 0% - all earnings retained.

q: Sales of an enterprise are Rs 32,00,000, variable costs are Rs 20,00,000 and fixed costs are Rs 4,00,000. The degree of operating leverage is:
An enterprise has earnings before interest and tax of Rs 14,00,000 and pays interest of Rs 4,00,000. Its degree of financial leverage is:
e: Degree of financial leverage = EBIT / (EBIT - Interest) = 14,00,000 / (14,00,000 - 4,00,000) = 14,00,000 / 10,00,000 = 1.4.

q: An enterprise has sales of Rs 26,00,000, variable costs of Rs 18,00,000, fixed costs of Rs 3,00,000 and interest of Rs 1,00,000. Its degree of combined leverage is:
e: Degree of combined leverage = Contribution / (Contribution - Fixed costs - Interest) = 8,00,000 / (8,00,000 - 3,00,000 - 1,00,000) = 8,00,000 / 4,00,000 = 2.0.

q: The degree of financial leverage of an enterprise is 2.4. If its earnings before interest and tax increase by 15%, its Earnings Per Share will increase by approximately:
e: Financial leverage magnifies EPS changes: percentage rise in EPS = DFL x Percentage rise in EBIT = 2.4 x 15% = 36%.

q: An enterprise is said to be over-capitalised when:

options.A: Its paid-up share capital exceeds its reserves and surplus
options.B: It has raised more capital than the cost of its fixed assets
options.C: Its current assets exceed its current liabilities by a wide margin
options.D: The capitalised value of its earnings is less than the amount of capital actually employed, so that the actual rate of return on its capital is lower than the prevailing rate of return for similar enterprises

e: An enterprise is over-capitalised when its earnings, capitalised at the prevailing fair rate of return, are worth less than the capital actually employed, so its real rate of return lags behind comparable enterprises.

q: Current assets of an enterprise are Rs 21,00,000 and its current liabilities are Rs 7,00,000. Its current ratio is:
e: Current ratio = Current assets / Current liabilities = 21,00,000 / 7,00,000 = 3 : 1.
